newsitem.title: UK: Rain hits Eastern Europe's grain crop potential.
newsitem.headline: Rain hits Eastern Europe's grain crop potential.

text.p: Central and Eastern European farmers could lose hundreds of thousands of tonnes of grain after recent widespread flooding, according to government and trade sources in the region.
More rain and flooding is on the way but with crops in many areas already badly hit, the scope for further quantitative damage is limited.
But fears over grain quality triggered sharp price rises on Budapest's Commodity Exchange.

Hungary's wheat crop, while almost certain to reach a targetted five million tonnes after last year's 3.9 million, was likely to be the lowest quality in many years, trader Istvan Grebats of Termin brokerage said.
"We have heard of very bad quality in some places, excellent quality elsewhere, but almost nothing in between," said Gyorgy Pilaszy of trading company Agrograin.
Poland, already badly affected by flooding, was threatened with further floods on Friday.
"It is raining from Koszalin (in the north) through all of western Poland, with varying intensity," flood crisis committee spokesman Krzysztof Pomes said.
"The situation doesn't look good," he told Reuters at 1230 GMT, after several hours of rain in southwestern areas.
Deputy agriculture minister Jerzy Pilarczyk told Reuters in an interview on Thursday that so far 120,000 hectares (300,000 acres) of crops had been destroyed.
"The potential new flood wave will affect the same areas already under water," Pilarczyk said.
Rain in Yugoslavia in June and July seriously damaged crops over a wide area causing a 450 million dinar ($75.8 million) loss, a senior government official said on Friday.

"Heavy rains and hailstorms from June 17 to 20 and in the first (10 days) of July caused enormous damage to crops in Vojvodina and central Serbia," Jan Kisgeci of the federal Agriculture Ministry said.
"The damage is still being evaluated but according to first estimates the loss is some 450 million dinars," he told a news conference.
In the grain growing region of Vojvodina 8.5 percent of total arable lands were hit by bad weather.
In Romania recent rains also hit crop quality, an official said on Friday.

"The quality of the wheat harvested over the past week is low. Our wheat might not be in very big demand for export this year," Vasile Duta, general manager of the National Agency for Agricultural Products, told Reuters.

The Romanian agriculture ministry expects a total wheat crop of 7.07 million tonnes in 1997, almost double last year's. Duta said heavy rains in recent days affected crop quality, with falling gluten content and increased humidity in the grains.

Rain fell overnight across the flood-swept Czech Republic and storms expected at the weekend could trigger a new wave of the flooding that has devastated parts of the south and east, forecasters said on Friday.

Problems with the weather are not solely the preserve of central and eastern Europe. Grain harvesting in western Europe came to a standstill this week due to rain in most producing areas, after a prolonged spring drought.

Southern hemisphere farmers face potential damage from the developing "El Nino" weather pattern which is linked with drought in Southern Africa and Australasia. And Chicago corn futures opened sharply higher on Friday due to persistent dry weather in parts of the U.S. midwest.
